query: For single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, which requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and may lack the strength and structural integrity needed for service, what single intervention could lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention and its mechanism, predict its performance compared with conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, define the relevant preparation and service boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and describe a controlled preparation, integrity, and long-duration exposure experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small, volatile sintering‐aid additive (specifically, around 0.3 wt% Li2CO3) into high‐purity ZrB2 powder will enable a transient liquid phase during pressure‐assisted sintering that lowers the processing temperature (from >2300 °C to around 1700–1800 °C). This transient liquid will promote enhanced particle rearrangement and densification, significantly reducing residual porosity and minimizing nucleation sites for liquid penetration during plating, thereby improving the long‐term integrity against hole formation.
generation.material_initial_state: High‐purity, single‐phase ZrB2 ceramic powders that conventionally require sintering at temperatures above 2300 °C and display relatively coarse microstructures with microporosity prone to liquid infiltration.
generation.intervention: Doping the ZrB2 powder with a low concentration (~0.3 wt%) of Li2CO3.
generation.conditions: Perform pressure-assisted sintering (e.g., using SPS or a similar method) in an inert atmosphere at a reduced temperature in the range of 1700–1800 °C with a short dwell time to prevent excessive grain growth, ensuring complete densification and minimal residual additive content.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a transient Li2O-rich liquid film (derived from the decomposition of Li2CO3) at the particle contacts which promotes localized plastic deformation, improved mass transport, and grain rearrangement. The transient liquid phase helps fill interparticle voids and, upon its disappearance, leaves behind a dense, refined microstructure with diminished porosity.
generation.mechanism: At the reduced sintering temperature, the Li2CO3 additive decomposes early to form a Li2O-based liquid that temporarily wets the ZrB2 particles. This liquid phase lowers interfacial energy barriers and facilitates enhanced particle rearrangement and local densification via capillary forces. As the temperature stabilizes, the liquid phase evaporates or reacts completely, yielding a single-phase ZrB2 with reduced microporosity that is less susceptible to liquid infiltration during subsequent plating processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally sintered ZrB2 (≥2300 °C), the Li2CO3-doped samples will achieve full densification at 1700–1800 °C with a significantly refined grain size (estimated reduction of ~50% relative to conventional processing) and lower residual porosity. This will manifest as improved mechanical strength and a marked reduction in the initiation of holes or component failure under prolonged liquid plating bath exposure.
generation.baseline: Conventional pure ZrB2 sintered at temperatures above 2300 °C, which typically exhibits larger grains, higher residual porosity, and more pathways for liquid infiltration, leading to eventual component failure during extended exposure to liquid plating baths.
generation.boundary: The proposed intervention is applicable only to high-purity single-phase ZrB2 ceramics processed under controlled pressure-assisted sintering conditions. Care must be taken to optimize the Li2CO3 level so that it enhances densification without leaving contaminant residues or forming undesirable secondary phases.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on (1) evidence from UHPS studies (PMC8867202::web::031::conclusion) that reduced sintering temperatures via mechanical deformation and enhanced densification can yield refined, fully dense ZrB2 and (2) findings in other ceramic systems (PMC11173780::web::018::4_conclusions) where a transient liquid (via sintering aids) lowers sintering temperature and improves densification. What is new here is the extension of a transient, self-fluxing additive approach to pure ZrB2 to both lower sintering temperature and minimize porosity—thus potentially reducing vulnerability to liquid plating baths. Uncertainty remains regarding the complete removal of Li-based residues after sintering and whether the transient phase mechanism will function as effectively in ZrB2 as it does in oxide ceramics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of high-purity ZrB2 powder doped with ~0.3 wt% Li2CO3 and a control set with no additive. Using pressure-assisted sintering (e.g., SPS), process both sets at a target temperature of 1700–1800 °C under otherwise identical conditions. After sintering, perform comprehensive microstructural (grain size and porosity via SEM, porosimetry) and phase purity (XRD) characterizations. Subject both sample sets to a prolonged liquid plating bath exposure under simulated service conditions and subsequently evaluate mechanical properties (hardness, fracture toughness) and inspect for the formation of holes.
measurements: Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and porosimetry for microstructural analysis
Long-duration exposure tests in a standardized liquid plating bath
Chemical analysis to check for residual Li or secondary phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Li2CO3-doped ZrB2 samples do not show significant densification at the reduced sintering temperature (i.e., if they exhibit similar porosity and grain size as the conventionally sintered control), or if XRD/chemical analysis reveals the presence of deleterious secondary phases or residual Li, or if the doped ceramics are not demonstrably more resistant to hole formation during plating bath exposure, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, we prepared MnO2-doped aluminosilicate ceramics and disclosed that a 0.3 wt.% addition of MnO2 can sufficiently make the aluminosilicate ceramics sintered at 1150 °C possess identical flexural strength as the undoped counterpart sintered at 1200 °C (M-0-1200 sample). The lowest water absorption reaches 0.05%, merely one-tenth of the water absorption for the M-0-1200 ceramic sample. The added MnO2 can decrease both the pore size and total pore volume, and enhance the sintering densification; this is probably because the MnO2 transforms into a liquid phase in the sintering process and flows into the gap between grains which removes the gas inside the pores and fills the pores, suppressing the generation of pores and the abnormal growth of grains. Also, this study demonstrated a facile method, doping with MnO2 using mechanical stirring at room temperature, to lower the water absorption, enhance the flexural strength, and reduce the sintering temperature concurrently, which has a promising value for practical ceramic production.

AbstractZrB2–HfC ceramics have been fabricated using the liquid phase sintering technique at a sintering temperature as low as 1750 °C through the addition of Ni. The effects of HfC addition on the microstructure and mechanical properties of ZrB2–based ceramics have been investigated. These ceramics were composed of ZrB2, HfC, Ni, and a small amount of possible (Zr, Hf)B2 solid solution. Small HfC grains were distributed among ZrB2 grain boundaries. These small grains could improve the density of ZrB2–based ceramics and play a pinning role. With HfC content increasing from 10 wt % to 30 wt %, more HfC grains were distributed among ZrB2 grain boundaries, leading to weaker interface bonding among HfC grains; the relative density and Vickers hardness increased, and flexural strength and fracture toughness decreased. The weak interface bonding for 20 and 30 wt % HfC contents was the main cause of the decrease in both flexural strength and fracture toughness.Keywords: ZrB2–HfC ceramics, hot pressing, sintering aid, microstructure, mechanical properties

In summary, fully‐dense and finer‐grained ultra‐high temperature ZrB2 ceramics were successfully fabricated under ultra‐high pressure at low temperature. The dominant densification mechanism was proposed and proved as the plastic deformation‐induced dislocation multiplication and grain boundary sliding. The proportion of dislocation cells, substructures, and small‐angle grain boundaries gradually increased when the sintering temperature reached the critical temperature of 1450 °C. ZrB2 sintered under 15 GPa at the optimized temperature of 1450 °C holding 10 min showed full density, fine microstructures, high dislocation density, and excellent mechanical properties. The grain size of as‐sintered ZrB2 ceramics decreased ≈56% compared with the raw powder. The microstructure observation after indentation and properties characterization after heat treatment proved that the high dislocation density, finer grain size, and high prestress induced by UHPS contributed the enhancement of mechanical properties.
